newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FORECAST - Brazil Aug trade gap seen near $300 mln.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Brazil Aug trade gap seen near $300 mln.

text.p: Poorer-than-expected exports, possibly due to anticipated changes in tax rules that will benefit exporters, should push Brazil's August trade deficit to about $300 million, analysts said.
The Senate is expected to vote on Thursday whether to exempt certain exports from a special tax, known as the ICMS. If the exemption is approved, it should boost exports of a variety of goods.

"Exporters could be holding back waiting for approval of the ICMS in the Senate," said Marcelo Carvalho, JP Morgan's chief economist in Brazil. "If this is the case we could see a possible payback in coming months but not enough to undo the underlying trend of trade deterioration."
Coffee and soy bean shipments are said to be piling up at Brazilian ports in anticipation of the vote.

The Ministry of Commerce and Industry released an August export figure of $4.38 billion, which fell short of expectations of $4.5 billion. The ministry is expected to release August imports and the trade balance for the month sometime in the next two weeks.

A Reuter survey of eight Brazilian brokerages and research firms forecast an August deficit of $311 million. Prior to the release of export figures last week, the same survey forecast a $210 million deficit for August.
Although economists have raised their deficit projections for August, they said there was nothing alarming about Brazil's trade picture at the moment.

"Seasonally adjusted, it looks like the figures are keeping within a recent trend of monthly deficits of between $400 million and $500 million and that is easily financed," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC Bank in Brazil.
Analysts added that the August result should be better than July's $334 million shortfall, if only because August had one less working day.
But they point out that deficits over the past two months have come at a time when Brazil should be posting healthy trade surpluses due to exports of soy and other agriculture crops.

"From here on out, the trade accounts will be pressured because of lower commodity exports and rising imports of consumer goods as retailers get ready for Christmas," said an economist at a Sao Paulo investment bank who requested anonymity.
This week's release of exports for the first week of September provided a glimpse of things to come on Brazil's trade front, economists said.
The government said exports for the week were $941 million, giving a $188.2 million daily average, down from a $199 million daily average in August.
